I wish I could like Hereditary more. It attempts to tap into a fear not engaged with enough: that is, hereditable disease/mental illness. Formerly, such diseases were incorporated into horror in a mystical or religious way, birth defects being a prime example. Such defects were alternatively viewed as divine or a curse, either being an elevation from normal existence. Now (by that I mean at least since the modern synthesis), with the scientific comphrension of herediability, a new sort of horror has arose. The horror of potentially damning your offspring to a life of suffering, though by no personal fault of your own. In this film, some scenes capture this anxity brilliantly, both from the mom and her son's perspective. Unfortunately, these scenes are invariably undermined by less-than-great acting or by being retroactively neutured (e.g. made into a dream). Even if the individual scene was allowed to breath (rarely), the overarching themes (doll-house, A24 etc), which weren't pulled together well, hampered the cinematography. I did like that the family (namely the father) was supportive, the "curse" of disease can strike anyone. The ending was also provocative (especially when read through the lens of mental illness). Also, maybe its just me (or that I had this movie partially spoiled), but it really wasn't that scary! Probably because it felt so pastiche?

A symphony of gimmicks and muddied waters. I hate to be that person again…. but I genuinely didn’t enjoy this at all. For me, possession/satanic cults and rituals as a trope usually lead to something, to some greater overarching plot. And although not everything needs to have a deeply moving message, this movie unfortunately feels like it lost its own in the process. A lot of the more memorable and twisted scenes only work and have the impact they do because they leverage that early gravitas of the potential exploration of grief, lose of youth/bodily autonomy, familial cycles and traumas, etc. But this film never truly makes that turn around back to the point it initially latched onto and conveniently lets go for the sake of shock factor. I’ll totally be the person to give the actors their flowers, and some of the scenes would not have functioned as such great pieces of storytelling if it was not for the camerawork. But aesthetics and talents can only take you so far. I think this has consistently been my gripe with Ari Aster is he has such great ideas and his attention to detail is insane, but are his grandiose projects fleshed out to begin with? Honestly no. He relies on the conversation and pushing the limits of what horror can be, which I do frankly respect him for; but again this, like a lot of his other work let me go as easily as it grabbed me. And genuinely I’m left with 0 takeaway from this… maybe I’m the problem

About 6 months ago,  the world started seeing advertisements for a film that was touted as “a game changer” and “the scariest movie ever made”. Are we given any reason Annie wears guilt or that she “adds stress” to her family? Other than feeling the way she does about her mother, we’re given none whatsoever. So what is Hereditary ? An indulgent genre piece that’s not only missing an hour of family drama that would emotionally tie things together (as confessed by the director), it’s spiritually empty. Years ago, I played in a pretty crappy punk band. Although we usually only played to friends (and, on one weird instance, a group of preschoolers), it taught me two valuable lessons about life: 1. Always leave your audience wanting more. 2. Never play every card you have in your hand. Sure, you might know twenty five original songs and a few covers--but that doesn't mean everyone there wants to fucking sit through it. After a while, even the most pleasurable of experiences will begin to drag, to grate, to become stale and monotonous. If I had any advice to give to Ari Aster, it would be to learn these two rules as quickly as possible. I really, really enjoyed this film as it began--and up until about the hour and a quarter mark, I was still sold and ready to rate this as one of the best movies I've seen this year. Hereditary, very early on, is unafraid to go to some incredibly dark places that a mainstream horror film--hell, even a mainstream film in general--is usually too much of a wuss to even approach. The delineation between the first and second acts in particular is so extremely uncomfortable, horrifying, and upsetting that it will likely be in my top ten sequences of the year, if not the decade. And then--like a third-billed band who decides to go fifteen minutes over their set time--it just. keeps. going. Rather than pick one specific thing and absolutely nail it, Aster and his production team here seem to want Hereditary to be absolutely everything within the horror genre--and in doing so, they end up flubbing ninety percent of it due to overreach. What was once slow, moody, and unbearably nervewracking disintegrates as the film stretches ever onwards into being just a plain-ol' unrelenting slog. Is this the story of a family falling apart? An accident that scars people for life? Mental illness? A creepy cult? A body horror film about possession? Yes, and we'll go well past our welcome in order to keep showing you and explaining to you more and more and more and more and... Forgive me. I don't think I've been this mad at a film since Suicide Squad--although for entirely different reasons. Aster has established himself with Hereditary as a masterful image maker. That is indeed remarkable. But if he wants to keep my interest, he's going to have to learn to rein himself in. Unfortunately, given the reception of so many others to this film, I'm afraid he's going to learn the wrong lesson.

Hereditary is a narratively hollow culmination of ideas Ari Aster wrote on many napkins over a decade, stashed in a shoebox, then pulled out and scattered down a staircase to make a script. It bounces around various genres, concepts, plots, and themes, then haphazardly staples them together with elements of Rosemary's Baby. What it does well is evoke inventively disturbing imagery, underscored by immense dread. Okay A24--we're done. No more of these half-realized genre pics, technical exercise, calling cards. May Under The Skin remain the only great film you've released(okay and Spring Breakers). So what's wrong with Hereditary ? It's cynical but not so obviously at first. The first half begins with quite an unexpected plot point and builds upon it with an eerie, grief felt, and almost at the edge of tears/laughter kind of atmosphere. It is refreshing that the film doesn't cheaply go for jump scares(make of that whatever you will) and god damn, Toni Collette is great. She's perfect for this kind of role, too bad it's stuck in a movie that in turn, leads her character into one of the most tired resolutions. And really, that's where this film comes undone. It is easy to figure out what exactly is going on and the scariest thing is that it'll confirm your own presumptions that this film has nowhere new to go. In fact, it lamely falls back on the kind of final half hour that dissolves first, into absurdity, and second, into cynicism. What does that leave us with? A technical exercise and nothing more. What the film had set up was perfectly fine, and hilariously, its playing off well worn tropes of the horror genre by sheer force of will. But what the film fucks up, is that horror in one way or another, has to have more than just a bunch of creepy happenings and then the most routine, lame, and tired explanation to all those creepy happenings. Why does the director rely on dollhouses? Because the shots look cool. Why mine mental illness? Who cares. The big bad in this feels like a cheat. One in which I didn't have a single care or devotion to. And the film leaves it at that, which is so frustrating. The best kind of horror films leave us by confirming that our fears and emotions are justified, even if they are strongly ambiguous. What Hereditary does is try to explain why we should be afraid or why we were afraid before. It doesn't add up and it doesn't have the heart, nerve, or audacity to accept that. It would rather seem ambiguous and deep, as if it were pulling one over the audience, but its last trick is predictable, lazy, old news.

Way too much going on at once here for it to work as much of anything. In this sense, it becomes obvious that Hereditary is from a first time director in Ari Aster, as he throws in just about every horror trope that has gained critical and financial success in the past five years. The film really does have it all: the slow, brooding pace, the ambient soundtrack that becomes unsettling from the eclectic percussion, the long takes with smooth camera movement, haunted house spooks and scares a la James Wan, occultism, a weird looking kid, exploration of grief/guilt through horror, etc. If that seems like a lot it is because it is, and the film is unable to really commit fully to what it wants to be, resulting in a jarring tone. It probably would have worked well had it fully committed to one of the multiple films going on here, but as it stands we have a story of grief and regret that goes completely off the rails. It is all an exercise in excess, a mishmash of what is "in" right now in horror. The camerawork in particular is somewhat infuriating, I'm all for clever camerawork but this film just felt gimmicky at times. Specifically, a shot where Collette's character returns to visit Jeanie, and as she walks down the hall the camera is upside down, only to smoothly flip when she passes to go right side up. Maybe trimming unnecessary shots like this will make it so your horror movie isn't two hours long, brutal when there's not many scares to be had. To be quite honest, I think I'm about sick of the A24 art house horror/thriller style that all feel about the same, relying heavily on the art house style. This is fine if you actually make a compelling film around it, but recent busts like It Comes at Night and now Hereditary make it clear that the style is stale and the film needs to be ACTUALLY SCARY if it wants to work. Hereditary is too complex for its own good. The real bummer about this is there are parts that are really great in the film, which makes me think that Aster one day will make a good horror movie if he learns to have a more focused vision. Toni Collette gives a wonderful performance, honestly the family as a whole is pretty solid at capturing what it feels like to struggle with loss. And a certain car scene is one of the more shocking moments I've seen in a film, an incredibly powerful (and, perhaps exploitative moment given where the film goes) moment that genuinely left me stunned for a good few minutes after. Hereditary could've been great if it decided to be a drama focused on grief, a haunted house movie (because boy does this at the end want to be The Conjuring so fucking badly), a weird pulpy occult film, a more straightforward ghost flick, or about family dynamics following a complicated loss, but not all at once. What we get is a bloated horror movie that is light on everything scary and compelling, instead bouncing around from theme to theme resulting in a climax that feels so out of left field it is almost laughable. Am I missing something here? The praise is baffling to me. This movie does literally nothing better than other movies recently have, the grief as horror is probably better in The Babadook, the spooky house moments pale to Wan's work, the occultism feels like a lazy way to end a film, and the family drama is much better in a film like A24's own Krisha. There's a good movie in here somewhere, it's just got way too much going on to really see.

"I just don’t want to put any more stress on my family." Annie Graham (Toni Collette) makes miniature models for a living, including ones that reflect her weird relationship with her recently-departed mother. The effects of that relationship carry over to her interactions with her conflicting-avoiding husband Steve (Gabriel Byrne), her bong-hitting son Peter (Alex Wolff), and her clucking daughter Charlie (Milly Shaprio). Charlie, was particularly close to her grandmother, and finds it hard to accept the love of her mother. When Annie discovers her mother was heavily into the occult, her influence only grows from beyond the grave. Hereditary is a movie that has a distinct midpoint, with two very different movies on either side (think of the shooting scene in "Boogie Nights"). The first half is about a family's pain, and how they work hard not to address it. The second is about the terror created when those family members go to extremes to heal that pain. So the former is a slow-paced drama while the latter is a quickening horror film. And that's the main problem with this film. First-time writer/director Ari Aster had a strong  story idea and a distinct vision for telling it. However, he likely should have done one or the other. With the film's slow-burn beginning, the air is let out of the horror balloon, which made the second half less effective. This movie is being billed as this generation's "Exorcist," which creates high audience expectations. But without the continued building pace needed to scare the shit out of us, things that would likely have stood out as set pieces are lost. There are some things Aster does very well. Annie's model houses are a running metaphor, and he utilizes long shots that make the family look like they inhabit one of them. And there some great tracking shots I'm still trying to figure out how he did them. But we likely could have traded some brooding, quiet moments for illustrating parts of the backstory rather than telling it. With the grandmother discussed but not really seen, she's more concept than character. There's also a moment where a connection is noted in a line of dialogue that exposes a throughline of revelations all the way to third act (at least it did for me). A fresh set of eyes in the director's chair might have been able to find these flaws and corrected them to deliver a scarier film. First of all, this film is not "this generation's 'The Exorcist.'" Nor is it "this generation's 'Rosemary's Baby'" for that matter. "Hereditary" doesn't come close to those classic horror films in terms of characterization or narrative coherence.  Toni Colette, Ann Dowd, and Alex Woolf all give very strong performances, and the film boasts some unusually creepy imagery, fabulous sound design (the doppler effect immerses us in the film, to the point that I swore I heard tongue clucking in the cab on the way home) and great sequences, rendering it a good, perhaps even very good, film. However, the story remains sketchy, and the ending in particular feels overwrought and unsatisfying, straining "suspension of disbelief."  There is not enough context for that resolution, as I saw it, so I felt stunned and a little let down. Which is really too bad, because the sequences leading up to it - directly after the "fire" scene - are extremely tense and quite frightening. The car scene with Peter and Charlie (I hope to see more of Milly Shapiro in future films!) is also brilliant & horrifying. It just doesn't come together **in terms of story.** Even the film's title is not clearly explained. There are intimations, but nothing is made clear. Don't get me wrong: ambiguity is fine; in fact, I usually love it. But "Hereditary" has too many loose threads to take it from very good to excellent. I will give it another watch, of course, to see if that changes for me. For now, I am glad I saw it in a theatre, and there is certainly lots to like, regardless of my critiques. Little bit of column A. Little bit of column Bad. This is the work of an adept technician with only a meager command of narrative and drama. Is ToniCollette-sploitation a thing? She's wild here. Hereditary possesses some impressive formal chops but the aesthetics have the misfortune of drawing attention to how lame the direction is when it's not trying to scare you. The mise en scene and uncanny dollhouse shots (especially those lateral tracks through walls!) I found to be aces, however, try to move the story along or do character work and you get hackneyed script or one dimensional direction. Note all the times a scene continues in an unmotivated slow zoom or begins on an object close up then pans to a character. These happen repeatedly and are more stylistic than revealing. Reaction shots are held beyond comfort although not in a gainful way; more in a way that has me asking 'is that all?'. Admittedly the camera movements contrast the stillness of the spooks for when they appear (frame movement vs movement in frames), but this technique communicates little more than its presence in the moment. The same can be said for the editing. Clipped scenes and dissolves, which seem more like choices made in conjunction with the score, a buzzing drone uniting mood and blurring time. Without spoiling anything, the film wants the audience to pendulate between two possible explanations up until the ending when it jettisons the more interesting (and fleshed out) of the two as more or less irrelevant. To this end, the narrative plays fast and loose with reality and portent, all the while whittling itself down to a literal but complex closure. Hereditary 's heart and head are in its play of light and shadows, but the interstitial tissue rots from neglect. (Edit. I have learned the original cut was much longer and contained elements I found lacking, so I could change my tune on the drama and narrative if I were to see it.)

I’m not saying that directors of horror films are better than other directors; I am saying that horror is a genre that is going to expose who’s got “it,” and who doesn’t. First-time feature director Ari Aster absolutely has “it” in this thriller about a woman named Annie (Toni Collette) who is dealing with the recent death of her mother when she begins to see spectral apparitions, and her family faces a variety of fresh terrors. Lurking around the edges of Aster’s story are possible metaphors for parents who fear what they might pass on to their kids—things like mental illness—but the thematic stuff is almost incidental. This is simply one creepy-ass piece of filmmaking, as Aster shows off an exquisite sense of where to put the camera so that an ominous glint of red light reflects in someone’s eye, or something unspeakable lurks in a dark corner of the frame. And he’s savvy enough at how to set up his narrative and his sound design so that a seemingly innocuous sound like a clucked tongue becomes a harbinger of doom. Hereditary gets a bit needlessly expository during its climax, part of an overall sense that there’s some pacing fat that could stand trimming. It’s absolutely worth that extra time, though, to put yourselves in the hands of someone who understands the way cinema can inspire profound unease.

This is the best horror film I've seen since The Witch, and yet again A24 demonstrates that it's making all the right moves in order to champion up-and-coming visionaries; cementing the names of the bright directors at the roots of each of their dark and bold features. Ari Aster is the name to remember here: Hereditary is a masterful and nightmarish film, chilling throughout and virtually unpredictable at every turn. At the heart of the feature is Toni Collette's commanding performance. Aster has described his goal to direct and evoke a kamikaze-like portrayal of the film's central role, and Collette doesn't ever shy from pushing this all the way. Her steadily unhinged performance does wonders for illuminating underlying tension in the story, as well as exuding the sheer brilliance we've come to expect from her. As often as the film scares, it also unsettles to the bone - a testament how visceral and unnerving its subject material can be. The film is minutely crafted with telling metaphors, and the familial melodrama fabric of the plot offers plenty both said and left unsaid. There's a sense of slow-burning and a conscious inevitability to these events, and yet the film's psychological components are also interwoven quite seamlessly. I was constantly intrigued, never at ease, and entranced by the progression of events - it's a film too good to discuss at length without fear of spoiling key details; at once troublesome to categorize. There are several genuinely horrifying moments, but also many instances of pure and recognizable grief, aforementioned melodrama, and the film's foreboding and relentlessly macabre atmosphere. As with all horror films, though, it'll be typically hard to please everyone. Having seen Eggers' The Witch at least five times now, I still find it difficult to convince certain skeptics (and jump-scare junkies) of its art and brilliance. To this entire crew's credit, Hereditary exemplifies a brilliant niche of subconscious-affecting horror, staying under your skin even after you've left the cinema; its chills reverberate the more you recall it to memory. The perfect type of disturbing, it's an experience that will be hard to shake for many. If I were to highlight one final detail here, it's the fact that the film itself is a self-effacing metaphor for its themes. Much like the grief and trauma that grips the Graham family, it's the insidious; the repressed, subtle and nuanced moments of distress and terror that linger long past the credits. (8.4/10)

Der wahre Horror entsteht für mich aber erst dann, wenn man aufhört die Figuren als Filmcharaktere zu sehen und versucht sich in sie hineinzuversetzen. Plötzlich wirkt nichts mehr wie klassischer Horror, sondern wie ein Albtraum, aus dem niemand mehr aufwachen kann. Dazu kommt eine Kameraführung die ihrer Zeit wirklich voraus war. Man merkt wie sehr sich neuere Filme, gerade Obsession oder Backrooms an dieser Art der Inszenierung bedienen. Ari Aster schafft es selbst ein völlig normales Haus so wirken zu lassen, als würde jede Ecke auf den perfekten Moment warten um dir die letzten zwei Jahre Therapie wieder zunichtezumachen. Das Geniale an Hereditary ist für mich, dass der Film auf zwei völlig unterschiedliche Arten funktioniert. Entweder man sieht ihn als kompromisslosen okkulten Horrorfilm oder als zutiefst verstörendes Familiendrama über Trauer, Schuld und psychische Erkrankungen. Und je genauer man hinhört was die Figuren erzählen und je mehr man auf die kleinen, fast unscheinbaren Details achtet, desto mehr öffnet sich der Film für Interpretationen. Es wirkt ab und an zufällige, aber viele Kleinigkeiten wirkten sehr bewusst platziert. Und dann kommt die letzte halbe Stunde... Ich saß wirklich nur noch auf der Couch und dachte: "Ich will mein Kuscheltier Ohnezahn wieder in den Arm nehmen." Manche Menschen schauen Horrorfilme mit Popcorn. Ich mit emotionalem Support-Drachen. Hereditary ist einer dieser Filme die nicht enden, wenn der Abspann läuft. Er bleibt im Kopf, kriecht langsam unter die Haut und lässt einen noch Tage später über Szenen nachdenken, die man beim ersten Mal vielleicht gar nicht richtig wahrgenommen hat. Und genau das macht für mich großartigen Horror aus. All in All, müsst Ihr Wissen!
